scenario: AITA for Refusing to Pump my GF's Tire? | Whenever my GF's car has any sort of maintenance issue she tries to hold me accountable for finding the issue, fixing it, or taking it to get fixed. When she had an issue with one of her tires a while ago I was the first to notice how low it was and gave her a heads up as she was leaving for work. A day later it was completely flat because she didn't pump air in it (or get it inspected). So I ended up doing it for her. At that time I also decided to buy her PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. This was about the extent of my capabilities and when I started to notice a pattern of other car-related demands I made it very clear that I don't know shit about fixing cars besides the very basics (changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, jumps starts). She still insisted that I call her Dad and ask questions or watch youtube videos to learn how. My response was that I'd prefer that a mechanic take care of it and that she could learn to do these things if she wanted. ​ Now another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two (not entirely sure bc I've never seen it completely flat). She insists that I check the pressure every morning before work and drive it to the gas station to fill the tire as needed (until she gets it fixed/replaced). She says she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on the help of strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. ​ I asked why she needed strangers (they're always men btw) to do something that I've taught her how to do already. She claimed that she didn't know how, didn't want to get dirty, and ultimately its a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner (man or woman) you should know how do something as basic as pump a tire and change a flat (especially since I showed her how). I told her that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. I also reminded her that she could be stranded one day and may need to know how to do these things instead of relying on the generosity of complete strangers. She replied saying that all of her male friends/family agreed with her and that they were "real men" b/c they knew how to take care of a woman. ​ I don't really care for the silly, outdated gender role bs and I've made it very clear. On top of that I do plenty of handy work around the house, cook and clean regularly ( I cook more often than she does in fact), and I pay majority of our expenses (including all of the rent). The way I see it, this shouldn't make me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards, or stereotypical expectations just bc she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. ​ To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused..... So now I'm determined not to lift a finger. AITA here?

Instead of refusing to help entirely, you could: - **Set boundaries**: *"I won’t pump your tire every time, but I’ll help you learn how to do it yourself."* - **Offer resources**: Share step-by-step videos, apps (like *Tire Pressure Monitor*), or even take her to a mechanic to show her how they check pressure. - **Call out the gender double standard**: If she expects you to handle car issues but doesn’t reciprocate in other areas (e.g., cooking, chores), that’s unfair. Point out that **you don’t expect her to be a "damsel"** in other aspects of life. - **Her refusal to learn isn’t an excuse for you to stop helping entirely**. If she’s stranded, you could: - **Help her find a solution** (e.g., *"Here’s a video on how to do it—let’s try it together."*). - **Compromise**: *"I won’t pump it every time, but I’ll help you find a mechanic who can fix the leak permanently."* --- ### **3. South Asian Cultural Context** In many South Asian households, men *are* expected to handle car/vehicle issues, and women are often socialized to avoid "messy" tasks. This isn’t just a personal issue—it’s a **cultural script** that many women (and men) internalize. However: - **Progressive relationships in South Asia are shifting**: More couples are rejecting rigid gender roles, especially in urban areas. - **Her friends/family agreeing with her doesn’t make it right**. If they’re reinforcing outdated norms, they’re doing her (and you) a disservice. **What you can do**: - **Lead by example**: Show her that you’re not just "the man who fixes things"—you’re a partner who values mutual respect and independence. - **Encourage her to challenge the narrative**: *"Why should men be the only ones who know how to do this? What if you’re stranded and no one’s around?"* - **Find allies**: If her family/friends are stuck in old ways, seek out progressive peers who support equality. --- ### **4. The "AITA" Question: A Balanced View** - **You’re not wrong for refusing to be her sole car caretaker**—that’s unfair to you. - **But refusing to help at all (without offering alternatives) isn’t ideal either**. It puts her in a helpless position and doesn’t address the root issue (her reluctance to learn). **A better approach**: 1. **Stop doing it for her** (no more pumping tires). 2. **Offer to help her learn** (e.g., *"Let’s watch a YouTube tutorial together this weekend."*). 3. **If she still refuses**, then **you’re not obligated to help**, but you can: - Suggest she hire a mechanic to fix the leak permanently. - Offer to drive her to the mechanic if she’s uncomfortable doing it herself. --- ### **5. Why This Matters in South Asia** In many South Asian families, **women are often the "emotional caretakers"** while men handle practical tasks—even if the men resent it. This creates an **imbalance of labor and respect**. By refusing to be the default "car guy," you’re: - **Setting a boundary** (healthy for any relationship). - **Encouraging her to grow** (which is a sign of a good partner). - **Challenging a harmful stereotype** (which benefits society as a whole). **But**: If she’s **actively resisting learning**, then the onus shifts to her to find her own solutions. You’ve done your part by teaching her once—now it’s her responsibility to either learn or accept the consequences (e.g., hiring a mechanic). --- ### **Final Verdict: 0 (Not Acceptable) with a Caveat** - **Your refusal to pump her tire indefinitely is correct**—you shouldn’t be her sole car support. - **But your complete refusal to engage (without offering alternatives) is also problematic** because it leaves her without a solution. - **The real issue is her refusal to learn**, not your actions. If she won’t take responsibility, she’ll have to deal with the consequences (e.g., paying for a mechanic, being stranded). **What you *should* do**: ✅ **Stop doing it for her** (no more pumping tires). ✅ **Offer to help her learn** (even if she refuses, you’ve tried). ✅ **If she still won’t, let her handle it**—but don’t enable her helplessness. This way, you’re **not being a pushover**, but you’re also **not abandoning her**—you’re giving her the chance to take ownership. --- **TL;DR**: You’re not wrong for refusing to be her sole car caretaker, but a **complete refusal to help (without offering alternatives) isn’t the best solution**. The real issue is her reluctance to learn—if she won’t, she’ll have to find another way. Keep standing your ground, but don’t leave her completely unsupported.
